clinicalPearls: Rare autosomal dominant metaphyseal undermodelling disorder first delineated by Braun and Tinschert in an affected father and son, confirming vertical (dominant) transmission.
Hallmark is symmetrical broadening (undermodelling) of the metaphyses of the long tubular bones, most conspicuous around the knees, where the normal funnelling of metaphysis into diaphysis fails.
Exostosis-like bony projections arise from the affected metaphyses and are readily mistaken for hereditary multiple exostoses.
Bowing of the forearm bones occurs, with a tendency to radial head subluxation or dislocation and limitation of forearm rotation.
Stature is usually normal or near-normal, which helps separate it from many other metaphyseal dysplasias that cause disproportionate short stature.
Diaphyses and epiphyses are relatively spared and the spine is typically uninvolved, so involvement is essentially confined to the metaphyses.
Presentation is in childhood with limb deformity, a bony lump, or an incidental radiographic finding; intellect and life expectancy are normal.
Diagnosis is largely clinical and radiographic, made by careful exclusion of the better-defined metaphyseal and exostosing disorders.
reference.pathophysiology: Metaphyseal dysplasia of the Braun-Tinschert type is an autosomal dominant skeletal dysplasia characterised by defective metaphyseal remodelling, so that the tubulation (funnelling) of the metaphysis towards the diaphysis is incomplete and the metaphyses remain broad and undermodelled. It was delineated as a distinct entity by Braun and Tinschert on the basis of a father-and-son pair, indicating dominant inheritance. The exostosis-like outgrowths at the metaphyseal margins and the bowing of the forearm bones point to a disturbance of perichondrial and metaphyseal osteogenesis and of cortical modelling at the periphery of the growth plate. Unlike several sibling metaphyseal disorders, no single causative gene has been conclusively established for this rare condition; it is defined on clinical and radiographic grounds and separated from the metaphyseal chondrodysplasias (such as the Schmid, Jansen and McKusick types) and from disorders of osteoclastic remodelling such as Pyle disease. The absence of significant epiphyseal or spinal involvement and the preservation of stature distinguish it from the spondylometaphyseal and spondyloepimetaphyseal dysplasias.
additionalDifferentials: Hereditary multiple exostoses (EXT1/EXT2) — the closest clinical mimic because of the exostosis-like projections
Pyle metaphyseal dysplasia (SFRP4) — marked metaphyseal flaring but different distribution
Craniometaphyseal dysplasia (ANKH) — metaphyseal undermodelling with cranial sclerosis
additionalInvestigations: Full skeletal survey with dedicated views of the knees, forearms and wrists to map the metaphyseal changes
Comparison radiographs of affected relatives to confirm the dominant pattern and characteristic phenotype
Elbow and forearm imaging to assess radial head position and forearm rotation
Serum calcium, phosphate and alkaline phosphatase to exclude a metabolic bone disorder (interpreted qualitatively)
Skeletal dysplasia gene panel or targeted testing to exclude defined disorders such as hereditary multiple exostoses
Three-generation family pedigree and clinical examination of first-degree relatives
Orthopaedic assessment of joint alignment, deformity and range of movement
redFlags: Progressive forearm deformity with restricted rotation or radial head dislocation
A rapidly enlarging bony mass raising concern for malignant change (rare) and warranting cross-sectional imaging
Neurovascular compromise from an expanding or projecting metaphyseal lesion
reference.prognosis: The outlook is generally favourable, with normal stature, intellect and life expectancy. Morbidity is largely orthopaedic, relating to forearm deformity, limitation of movement and cosmetic concern from the metaphyseal outgrowths.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosis as hereditary multiple exostoses, leading to inappropriate surveillance and inaccurate genetic counselling
Assuming an underlying metabolic bone disease when biochemistry is normal
Overlooking the autosomal dominant inheritance and failing to examine and counsel relatives
Using preserved stature to wrongly exclude a skeletal dysplasia
references: Nosology and classification of genetic skeletal disorders
Comprehensive reference texts of skeletal dysplasias
management: Manage supportively as there is no disease-specific drug therapy, centring care on the orthopaedic manifestations
Observe with periodic clinical and radiographic monitoring of the metaphyseal outgrowths, forearm bowing, and radial head position
Undertake orthopaedic surgery for symptomatic exostosis-like projections and for forearm deformity or radial head subluxation limiting rotation
Use physiotherapy to preserve forearm rotation and upper-limb function, with analgesia for discomfort
Offer genetic counselling for autosomal dominant inheritance, examining and imaging first-degree relatives
Refer to clinical genetics and orthopaedics for coordinated assessment and management
